podcast.body: Written by Jerry Casale in 1979, "Whip It" became Devo's first and most popular radio hit, featured on their third album, "Freedom of Choice." The song satirized American optimism about easily overcoming any problem. During performances, the band was visually distinctive, wearing black shorts, sleeveless black turtlenecks, and red plastic "flower pots" on their heads. "Cassali wrote the song in 1979. He was satirizing American optimism about whipping any problem that came our way."

podcast.body: The song "Whip It" was intended by a figure referred to as "Mother's Boss" to provide a critique or "kick in the butt" to President Jimmy Carter. This was motivated by Mother's Boss's concern that Ronald Reagan would win the 1980 election, which ultimately occurred. Musically, the song is described as simultaneously nonsensical, disoriented, and catchy, proving to be an annoyance to parents. It also served as a significant bridge, connecting the prevailing sounds of the 1970s with the emerging synth-driven pop music of the 1980s. Originating from the Ohio band Devo, "Whip It" achieved a peak position of number 14 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart in 1981. "The song is all at once nonsensical, disoriented, catchy, and annoyance to parents and a bridge from the sounds of the 70s to the synth driven pop of the 80s."
